Felix had been in enough trials by now to know better than to ignore the man’s instincts. He followed him toward the Eyrie’s doors. Inside, the Eyrie was eerily still. Books. Way too much sand. A lone generator, cold and ignored. And a pile of rubble where half of a staircase used to be. “Looks like the walkway above collapsed,” Felix murmured, eyes tracing the damage. “Took part of the stairwell with it. I wasn’t even aware the landscape could collapse like that in a trial.” “Things have been weird lately. Who knows what’s possible anymore.” The Eyrie had always been a weird mix of hideous planning and impressive masonry. Still, this was new. He caught himself studying the fault lines, noting where the arch had folded under its own weight — a perfect storm of tension and force — when Dwight’s voice cut through his thoughts, reminding him why they were there. “Hello?” A sound broke the quiet. Small. Choked. Like someone trying to stifle a cough. Felix froze mid-step, spine straightening instinctively. “Okay. That I heard.” Dwight was already turning toward the rubble, expression sharpening. It was an odd place to hunker down. Too exposed, no clear escape route. Although, if Jill was outside running Nemesis in circles, and he and Felix were right there... “David?” he called out, tone tight. “’m here,” came the thin reply — warped by grit and pressure, but unmistakably human. “Could use a hand, tho.” Felix’s head snapped toward the rubble, alarm flickering beneath his usual calm. “Did that just come from inside the collapse?” “Wait—shit,” Dwight surged forward without waiting for confirmation, boots kicking up sand. “Are you okay?! What happened?” No reply at first. Just the dull sound of stone shifting as David let his head rest against his arm again — too drained to move, too relieved not to. His body shook once, tension flaring and failing all at once. “Just get me out of here,” he muttered. “ Carefully . This shit is held together by spite.” Dwight and Felix traded a glance — silent, serious — before dropping to assess the pile. “We’ve got you,” Dwight said, already brushing grit away with careful hands and moving to grip at the stones. “Just stay with us.” David barely exhaled. A thread of breath. A flicker of disbelief. Help had come. Now all they had to do... was not kill him with it. Chapter 3 – Breakpoint The digging inevitably slowed after a time. Not because they were tiring — but because the pile was starting to respond. Felix had been directing the work with surgical precision, calling out load-bearing stones and picking targets with care, but even then... progress was agonizingly slow. Dwight’s idle chatter had kept David distracted for a while, the relief of not being alone having given him something else to focus on, but it did little to disguise the feeling of weight shifting as they worked. Every piece of rubble shifted something. Each stone removed sent new tremors through the makeshift tomb, and David felt it everywhere. The weight on his chest didn’t ease. If anything, it pressed in harder, like the structure above was getting impatient. Every time he exhaled, the space around his ribs compressed a little more. Tiny, incremental shifts. No sudden movements. Just the slow, inevitable collapse of geometry. Felix called something from above — an update, maybe. Dwight's voice replied, closer now, strained and anxious. David couldn’t make out the words. All he could hear was stone — the subtle grind of weight against weight. The whisper of pressure shifting in search of somewhere else to land. His right shoulder had started to burn. The numb, heavy blankness of his pinned arm was waking up again — coming back to him in flashes of static pain. Each inhale was a losing battle. Each exhale left him less to work with. The air that left his lungs didn’t come back — not fully. The space around him shrank by fractions, inch by inch, until it felt like the rubble was learning to breathe with him. Like a snake coiling tighter with every motion, the stones above stole space his body couldn’t reclaim. The panic didn’t crash down all at once. It seeped in quiet at the edges, crawling like cold fingers along the base of his skull. He pushed it back as best he could every time it flared up, but it kept coming back. He could feel the pile sliding. Not the big rocks. Not yet. Just the little ones. Pebbles crawling over his arm. Grit dusting down into the hollows of his collarbone. Something sharp shifted under his ribs — he couldn’t tell if it was a rock or a cracked bone. The dust thickened, burning his eyes, clawing its way down his throat. He coughed again, this one violent enough to spike fresh pain through his chest. Still, he stayed quiet. The words wanted out. He locked them behind his teeth. “...getting close,” Dwight cut through from above. “I think I see his shoulder — yeah, that’s fabric. That’s him.” “Careful,” Felix warned. “Don’t pull — just clear around it.” David tried to nod. Couldn’t. The pressure was too tight. “You’re doing fine. Just... don’t stop.” There was a tremble in his voice he couldn’t quite hide. “David?” Dwight’s voice lowered. “You okay?” He grunted. “Still here.” Technically true. It didn’t matter that he couldn’t draw a full breath anymore. Didn’t matter that every muscle left was burning just trying to hold his arm up between his skull and the stone. If he told them it was getting worse, they’d panic. If they panicked, they’d rush. If they rushed, they’d make a mistake. “I’m fine.
